title: The ghost shorelines of Chicago
takeaway: Of eight Native trail routes that Chicago streets still follow, only two ride the old beaches of glacial Lake Chicago.
story: At the end of the last ice age, glacial Lake Chicago stood 60 feet above today's Lake Michigan and covered 1,678 km² of what is now the city and its suburbs. As its outlet cut down, it fell in stages to 40 and then about 20 feet higher, leaving a beach ridge of sand and gravel at each stop. The ridges are still there, a metre or two high, under streets and rail lines.

Chicago often tells the story that its diagonal streets began as Native trails laid along those dry ridges. Testing 8,470 km of main streets against 1/3 arc-second elevation data finds that true for two routes: the Green Bay Trail along Clark Street and Ridge Avenue, which averages +1.34 m above the ground to either side, and the Calumet-area Ridge Road, at +2.27 m. The other six, Milwaukee, Lincoln, Archer, Ogden, Vincennes and Sauk Trail, sit no higher than an ordinary street.

Grid streets average +0.16 m and diagonal streets +0.31 m by the same measure, so most diagonals follow something other than a ridge: river crossings, portages and the shortest dry line between villages.
data_as_of: Elevation: USGS 3DEP, current as of October 2026; streets: Overture Maps release 2026-10-21.0; trail routes from sources read 26 Oct 2026
projection: Measured in UTM zone 16N (EPSG:32616) on a 10 m grid; the web layer is drawn in Web Mercator. The print plate is UTM zone 16N at 1:117,000.
alt: A map of Chicago and its suburbs from Wilmette to the Indiana line. Three pale blue bands west of Lake Michigan show the land covered by glacial Lake Chicago at its 640, 620 and 605 ft stages, reaching about 20 km inland at the widest, with a blue line along each old shoreline. Small tan patches mark ground standing a metre or more above its surroundings. Eight trail routes are drawn on today's streets: two in orange, the Green Bay Trail along the North Shore and Ridge Road near Lansing, follow the old beach ridges; six in dark grey, including Milwaukee, Lincoln, Archer and Ogden avenues, cross the lakebed without following a ridge.

method: Local relief is the ground minus a 400 m Gaussian average of itself, from the 10 m elevation model. Ridges on the map are lakebed ground at least 1 m above that average, generalized to 30 m.

Lake stages are connected floods at 640, 620 and 605 ft: ground counts as lakebed only if water at that level could reach it from Lake Michigan, and the flood is stopped where the lake spilled southwest through the Des Plaines and Sag valleys.

The crest test samples every primary, secondary and tertiary street every 50 m (8,470 km, 169,498 samples) on ground smoothed over about 60 m, and compares the ground under the road with points 150, 250 and 350 m to either side. Trail routes are drawn along the modern streets that the sources say follow them.
caveats: The trails wandered; the streets that follow them were straightened, so a route's score is for today's street, not the original path.
Low valleys behind the shore, such as the upper Des Plaines, fill too and may overstate the lake. No allowance is made for the slight tilt the land has taken since.
Rail and expressway embankments show as artificial ridges in the relief.
Stage elevations are textbook levels; published figures vary by a few feet.
credit: Map and analysis: John Kenny, in partnership with an AI coding agent that fetched the data and ran the analysis under his direction and review
